Three consequences discharged rather than absorbed: the gate now **reports its own cost** (a `planner-flags:` line so an arm is a positive statement in the artefact rather than the operator's memory — M0125-0011's repair applied to the TPC-H side — plus query-phase wall clock and cgroup v2 `memory.peak`, chosen over sampling `VmHWM` because the kernel's high-water mark cannot miss a spike between polls and survives the server being stopped); the knob's **failure direction was INVERTED** (unparseable and `on`/`true`/`yes` now land on the default, not off — once stage 2 is what ships, "off" is the deviation and the hazard becomes a typo silently handing an operator a planner production does not run, the mirror of the reasoning that made "off" right while the flag shipped off); and **`plan_snapshots/m0125-0005-relsize-default-stage2.txt` re-pins the baseline**, because `plan-gate` takes the newest snapshot by mtime and the flip's **22/22 divergence** would otherwise have surfaced as a regression on the next planner commit (post-flip: 22/22 MATCH, rc=0). The 22 moved plans are enumerated as **16 estimate-only** (flat `rows=1` → block-derived sizes) and **6 structural** (Q7 Q9 Q10 Q11 Q12 Q21), and Q12's single structural hunk — `Hash Join (INNER)` → `(INNER, build=left)` — is the stage-1 probe-side chooser acting on a cardinality signal it previously did not have, which is the 3.18× win's mechanism rather than just its size. The SF0.5 gate is **deliberately not re-run**, reasoned in §4.2: its criterion is `MISMATCH+CKMISMATCH+ERROR == 0`, the stage-2 arm scored 0/0/0 over all 99 queries, and the only delta to "unset post-flip" is a unit-tested parser branch that the post-flip spotcheck confirms reaches a real server. Stage 3 is **not** folded in (§I8 shadowing). Two ledger rows appended — the SF=1-for-SF0.5 substitution, and **phase 6.2's greedy join order, whose ledger row the design told this task to update and which turned out never to have been written**; it is meaningful for the first time now that the cold seed is a real cardinality rather than a constant. |
| 0125-0006 | [Set-operation chain associativity when branches are parenthesised (M0125-0006)](0125-0006-setop-chain-associativity.md) | accepted | SQL and PostgreSQL associate equal-precedence set operators LEFT to right; goopg did so only while the branches were bare. `parseParenthesisedSelectStmt` set `Parenthesized` at the closing `')'` and then absorbed a set-operator written AFTER that `')'` into the same chain, so the node claimed the user's parentheses covered an operator that appeared outside them and the planner's flattening loop treated the extended chain as one atomic operand — planning `A EXCEPT (B EXCEPT C)` for `(A) EXCEPT (B) EXCEPT (C)`. **A wrong-answer defect no row-count gate can see**: TPC-DS Q87 returned `47218` against PG's `47049` while both returned exactly one row, so the SF0.5 oracle, the nightly row anchors and the sweep harness were all structurally blind to it. The obvious repair — clear the flag — is refuted by a PG-verified probe (`X UNION (A EXCEPT B) UNION C` = `{2,3,9}`, but fully left-deep = `{2,9}`): the parentheses wrap a **prefix** of the chain, so the boundary must be a COUNT, not a bool. Fix = `SelectStmt.ParenBranches` (reset at the `')'` — load-bearing for `((B) EXCEPT (C))`, whose outer paren really does cover the inner level's absorbed operator) consumed by `parenBoundary`/`setOpSegment.cutAt`, which cuts the chain at the boundary instead of breaking, keying the existing save/clear/restore passes on `cutAt`. Cutting correctly exposed that goopg's fold has **no operator precedence at all** (`gram.y:825-826` makes INTERSECT tighter; bare `A UNION B INTERSECT C` is already wrong on pre-fix HEAD), so `setOpBindsTighter` declines the cut when the trailing operator binds tighter — locally correct precedence, and what keeps the change non-regressing. Accepted BY VALUE against PG 18.3: 17 executor cases + 9 parser AST pins, **proved to fail 10 subtests at `6c5c48ae` while every non-regression pin passed there**, and Q87 measured `47218 → 47049` on identical SF=1 data. Four pre-existing PG gaps the differential surfaced are deferred with ledger rows: precedence in bare chains (M0125-0016), `ORDER BY`/`LIMIT` hoisted out of a parenthesised first branch (M0125-0017), IN-list/EXISTS rejecting a parenthesised chain (M0125-0018), and `string_agg(… ORDER BY …)` ignoring its own ORDER BY (M0125-0019). |
| 0125-0007 | [PG-faithful date/time field decode (M0125-0007)](0125-0007-pg-faithful-date-field-decode.md) | accepted | `d_date = '2002-5-01'` matched **zero rows and raised nothing**, and three TPC-DS queries (Q16/Q94/Q95) answered `0 / NULL / NULL` because of it — all three under the same goopg checksum `512b5fdab820c47b` against three different oracle checksums. PostgreSQL's `DecodeDate`/`DecodeNumber` read each numeric run on its own, so `'2002-5-1'` and `'2002-05-01'` are the same date; goopg parsed with fixed Go layouts that demand zero padding, at ten-odd sites, several of which assumed padding as a **byte offset** (`s[4]=='-' && s[7]=='-'`, `s[:2]`, `s[5]`). The gap became a wrong answer rather than an error because `tryParseStringAs` reports a failed coercion by leaving the literal a string, and `KindTime` vs `KindString` is simply false. New leaf package `internal/pgdatetime` normalises the ISO numeric spellings in ONE place in front of the existing layout tables — with `DecodeNumber`'s own `flen >= 3` floor on the leading field, so the DateStyle-dependent forms stay loud errors instead of becoming silently-wrong dates — and every executor entry point routes through it. Found on the way: `ts_col = '2002-05-01 03:04:05'` also matched nothing (fully padded), because `parseTimeString` was tried first and anchors the stripped time at 1970-01-01. Acceptance landed the predicted signature (one checksum → three distinct) and identified what remains behind each query: Q16/Q94 over-count (M0125-0008, Q16 newly named), Q95 under-counts via a different mechanism (M0125-0023). |
| 0125-0008 | [A Semi/Anti join that published a layout it never produced (M0125-0008)](0125-0008-semi-anti-conjunction-residual.md) | accepted | Closes the **non-subset** defect: `EXISTS (…) AND NOT EXISTS (…)` over one outer relation returned MORE rows than either conjunct alone, so the answer was not even a subset of what the anti-join by itself admitted. The direction was the whole diagnosis — ANDing a conjunct cannot grow a result, so one conjunct had stopped filtering entirely rather than filtering wrongly. Bisects to a sharp threshold: correct at 1–2 base tables, wrong from **3**, which is where `rewriteMultiWayChain` packs the base joins into a `MultiHashJoin` and **OID-sorts its columns in place**. A Semi/Anti join emits the outer row only, and all three `unnest.go` construction sites plus `runJoinSearchBelowPinned` encode that by *copying* `Left.Output()` into a cached `schema` — the MHJ re-sort then left that copy a stale **permutation** of the layout its child actually produces. Widths still matched, so nothing detected it; the damage came from `reresolveJoinByName`, which re-resolves keys BY NAME against `j.Left.Output()`. For a semi/anti join *stacked on another one* that `Left` is the phantom layout, so the upper join's key landed on the wrong column (`ord`→index 2 = `dsk`), matched nothing, and — being an anti join — passed **every** probe row through. Reversing the two conjuncts moved the failure to the other join, confirming it is the topmost one that is neutered. Fix is one derivation, not a fifth refresh site: `Join.Output()` returns `Left.Output()` for Semi/Anti, since every writer set the cache to exactly that and the invariant is a definition rather than a choice — four passes had to remember the refresh and a fifth did not know the cache existed. **Also closes `M0125-0023` (Q95)**, filed separately on the reasoning "Q95 contains no `EXISTS`": that tracked the keyword, not the mechanism — Q95 stacks two `IN (subquery)` predicates over one outer rel and `IN`-unnest yields the same `JoinTypeSemi`, under-counting rather than over-counting only because the neutered conjunct was a semi join. Accepted by value against the git-tracked PG 18.3 SF0.5 oracle: Q16 `40dbec0df91d2438`, Q94 `04afc1b69831a5ea`, Q95 `e498634c02595c29` — all three CKMISMATCH→PASS. Subset sweep of all 13 SF0.5 queries containing `EXISTS`/`IN (SELECT)`: `PASS=9 MISMATCH=0 CKMISMATCH=0 ERROR=0 TIMEOUT=4`, the four timeouts pre-existing in prior sweeps. `make plan-gate` 22/22 TPC-H plans MATCH; spotcheck Q12=2 Q13=35. Both regression tests (executor four-arm isolation matrix + monotonicity invariant asserted directly; planner whole-tree structural invariant) verified RED with the fix reverted. **Deferred:** `NestedLoopIndexJoin.Output()` caches the same way and its refresher is gated on `costDrivenJoinOrder`, left alone pending its own reproducer. |
| 0125-0013 | [The MHJ leaf that was skipped twice over (M0125-0013)](0125-0013-mhj-posmap-filtered-leaf.md) | accepted | Closes TPC-DS **Q47** (`MISMATCH goopg=0 oracle=100` → 100 rows). The fix_plan item said to start in the windowed `v1`→`v2` self-join layers *above* the CTE, because RC-1b had made the CTE body "exactly correct — 661,185 rows = PG". It measured the body by **row count**, and the row count was never the broken half: goopg's 4-way join produced **332,240 rows, exactly PG's**, with every join predicate and filter applied correctly — only the *projection* read the wrong columns (`i_category`→`s_store_sk`, `d_year`→`s_county`, `d_moy`→`s_zip`, `i_item_sk`→`s_state`). `GROUP BY i_category` therefore grouped on `s_store_sk` (6 groups, not 11), 6-column and 4-column `GROUP BY` both collapsed to the same 29,617, and `rank() over (partition by …)` partitioned on columns unique per row so **`rn` was 1 for every row** (PG: 1..14) — making `v1.rn = v1_lag.rn + 1` the unsatisfiable `1 = 2`. The window layer was never broken; it was fed a permutation. Root cause is one arm of `buildBindingsPosMap`'s `collect` walker: the `*MultiHashJoin` case matched only bare `*SeqScan`/`*IndexScan`, but `pushSingleSourceFiltersIntoMHJTables` replaces `mh.Tables[i]` with `&Filter{Child: scan}` when it pushes a single-source conjunct down — and Q47's multi-column OR disjunction is exactly that, pushed into the `date_dim` leaf. A wrapped table matched nothing, **silently**, corrupting the map twice: no `scanEntry` (so its own columns keep their FROM-cumulative index) and **`off` never advanced** (so every table to its right is registered short by the wrapped table's width). Both halves close arithmetically on all eight observed columns. The inner remap was unaffected — and the row count with it — because `pushSingleSourceFiltersAfterRemap` creates the wrapper *between* `remapWithBindings` and `remapTopProjection`. Fix deletes the private switch in favour of `collect(t)`, which already handles both scan kinds identically, sees through the `*Filter`, and **declines** the whole remap on anything unclassifiable — the `default:`-arm hardening **RC-2 added for this exact failure mode and applied only to the outer walker**, never to the loop nested inside it. Sibling-paths (Rule #2) in a new position: outer walker ↔ its own nested inner walker. Sibling of M0125-0008 (same OID-sort origin, same widths-match invisibility) but a distinct mechanism — that was a stale cached layout, this is a walker that could not see a leaf. Both regression tests verified RED with the fix reverted, the bare-leaf one green on both sides to pin strict generalisation. `plan-diff` 22/22 MATCH (indices move, nodes don't); spotcheck Q12=2 Q13=35; SF0.5 window-family subset `PASS=7 MISMATCH=0 CKMISMATCH=0 ERROR=0`. **Deferred:** the full 99-query gate (three commits deep) and Q47's 8.4× STEP-0 runtime verdict, which no timing on this host can settle. |
| 0125-0009 | [`parserExprKey`'s type-name fallback, and the structural key that replaces it (M0125-0009)](0125-0009-parser-expr-key-structural.md) | accepted | The single highest-value TPC-DS fix of the programme, and the **third** recurrence of one failure mode: `parserExprKey` ended in `fmt.Sprintf("expr:%T", e)` — the Go TYPE NAME, no content — so all **seventeen** unenumerated `parser.Expr` types compared EQUAL to any other instance of themselves. Sibling `sum(CASE …)` aggregates therefore deduped onto one slot and every pivot column read the FIRST aggregate's value, **with the row count intact**, which is why the SF0.5 oracle, the nightly row anchors and ten sweep chunks all passed it; only M0124-0006's value comparison (rule D6a) found it, as 10 of 23 value-divergent queries. M0097-0003 (ColumnRef) and M0097-0032 (`count(*)` vs `count(*) FILTER`) had each patched one instance and left the fallback, so this closes the CLASS: a reflective structural walk over exported fields, skipping the unexported `pos` (the analogue of PG's `COMPARE_LOCATION_FIELD` no-op — load-bearing, or `GROUP BY <case>` would start raising a spurious 42803), routing nested nodes back through `parserExprKey` so normalisations still apply, sorted map rendering for determinism and path-marked cycle detection. Two explicit cases leaked the same way and are folded in — `FuncCall` dropped FILTER/OVER/in-arg ORDER BY/WITHIN GROUP/VARIADIC (`string_agg(x,',' ORDER BY a)` collapsed with `… ORDER BY b`), `CastExpr` dropped `Typmods`. The durable artifact is a two-part gate: a source scan that fails when a new `exprNode()` type is unregistered, and a per-field test asserting every exported field changes the key (exemptions must be declared with a reason, and a *stale* exemption also fails) — run against the old key it enumerates **40+ field-level collapses**. Measured at SF=1: 7 of the 10 evidence queries (Q2 Q40 Q43 Q59 Q50 Q62 Q99) are now value-identical to PG; Q21 and Q66 still diverge **for an independent reason** (both are FROM-subquery shapes → M0125-0010, and the two defects compose). Q97's collapse is gone and its residual gap isolated to a NEW defect filed as **M0125-0011**: goopg drops all but the first conjunct of a FULL OUTER JOIN's ON condition (two-key FOJ returns the single-key count, 2131274, where PG returns 836302 = 548694+287769−161). **Extended 2026-07-29 with §9 — M0125-0010, the same failure mode one layer down, now LANDED.** `remapSubqueryColumnRefs` (the FROM-subquery repair pass, called only from `planSubqueryRangeVar`) rebuilt EVERY bare-`ColumnRef` `Project` target by matching the ref's name against the child output schema and taking the first hit — but an `Aggregate` names its outputs after the aggregate FUNCTION, so `select * from (select sum(a), sum(b) from t) d` planned a child schema of literally `[sum, sum]` and both targets bound to slot 0, returning `sum(a)` twice. The pre-remap indices were verified already correct: the pass was not repairing damage, it was causing it. Fix = **verify-then-repair** — a target whose existing index is in range AND names the column the ref asks for is left alone (the only branch that can tell two same-named columns apart, so it must precede any name search); only an out-of-range index, or one naming a different column (the actual M0097-0058 leakage signature), is re-derived by name. A purely positional remap — which the pass's own doc comment claimed to implement — was rejected: it breaks any `Project` that reorders or subsets its child. Gate = 3 tests in `subquery_remap_test.go`, including the M0097-0058 leakage guard that stops the pass from being “simplified” away, and a control matrix of shapes that were already correct; four of six matrix rows fail against the old code, with `group by` failing as `[0 1 1]` — a partial collapse. Measured at SF=1: **all six carrier queries now match PG** (Q21 byte-identical, Q28 Q46 Q66 Q68 Q79 identical mod the separate `char(n)` padding gap). Q21 and Q66 needed BOTH fixes, so neither defect could be graded by “does the query match PG” alone. |
| 0125-0016 | [The set-operation fold has no operator precedence (M0125-0016)](0125-0016-setop-operator-precedence.md) | accepted | The other half of 0125-0006's class, and the same blind spot: a **wrong answer with a plausible row count**. PG's `gram.y:825-826` declares `%left UNION EXCEPT` then `%left INTERSECT`, so INTERSECT groups first and `transformSetOperationStmt` always sees INTERSECT runs already grouped. goopg flattened a chain into `(operator, operand)` segments and folded them **left-deep regardless of the operator**, so with no parentheses anywhere `A UNION B INTERSECT C` planned as `(A UNION B) INTERSECT C` — `{3}` where PG gives `{1,3}`. M0125-0006 had added `setOpBindsTighter`, but only the paren-boundary cut consulted it, so the *parenthesised* spelling was correct while the bare one stayed wrong; before that change the parenthesised spelling had been right only **by accident**, because flattening stopped early. Fix = a two-level precedence climb over the flattened list: `planSegment` (the existing cut/plan/restore dance, lifted out of the loop body verbatim), `applySetOp` (column-count check + `wrapSetOpBranchWithCasts` **re-based on the accumulated left operand**, which with grouping is no longer always the leftmost branch), and `foldSetOpRange`, where a leading INTERSECT run attaches directly to the accumulator and every later UNION/EXCEPT operand first absorbs the maximal INTERSECT run that follows it. `InnerSegmentCount` (M0097-0044) is treated as a **hard precedence barrier**, not just a sort/limit marker: the user's parentheses grouped those segments explicitly, so `(A UNION B ORDER BY 1) INTERSECT C` must not become `A UNION (B INTERSECT C)` — folding each side of the barrier separately gives that *and* preserves the invariant that `left` equals the inner compound when `wrapSetOpSortLimit` wraps it, which is why the fix is a range fold rather than a pre-pass. Accepted BY VALUE against PG 18.3 (port 65438): 17 cases in `setop_precedence_test.go` covering both precedence directions, `ALL` on either operator, multi-link and mid-chain INTERSECT runs, the UNION/EXCEPT tie, the barrier with `ORDER BY` and `ORDER BY … LIMIT`, and explicit parens overriding precedence the other way; **proved to fail 8 subtests at pre-fix `70e1ca61` while all four controls and the entire barrier suite passed there**. TPC-DS cannot reach the defect — Q8/Q14/Q38 are its only INTERSECT users and every chain is homogeneous, hence associative — and the SF0.5 set-op subset (Q23 Q38 Q49 Q87) came back checksum-identical to the HEAD sweep. The full 99-query gate was not run (its guard refuses under the live nightly batch, and the sweep's ~21 GB Q5 peak would not fit beside the wedged nightly server); recorded in the working set for the next quiet-host loop. |
| 0125-0017 | [The parenthesised head branch had nowhere to put its own ORDER BY / LIMIT (M0125-0017)](0125-0017-setop-head-branch-sort-limit.md) | accepted | The third member of 0125-0006's class and the worst-behaved: `(A ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 2) UNION ALL (C)` returned `{1,2}` against PG's `{1,2,9}` — the head branch's LIMIT was applied to the union, so **an entire UNION ALL branch vanished** while the row count stayed plausible. Root cause is the same missing structure as 0125-0006: goopg stores a set-op chain as a linked list, so the head branch and the whole compound are ONE node sharing ONE `OrderBy`/`Limit`/`Offset` slot, whereas PG's `select_with_parens` is a leaf operand carrying `opt_sort_clause`/`opt_select_limit` on its own node (`gram.y`). M0097-0044's `InnerSegmentCount` already answered the case where the parenthesised content was a compound, but **0 is its unset sentinel**, so it could not express the commonest boundary of all — the parentheses closing after the FIRST branch, i.e. after ZERO segments. Fix = `SelectStmt.InnerSortLimit`, one bit that makes `InnerSegmentCount`'s zero meaningful, set in `parseParenthesisedSelectStmt`'s single-branch arm (where the slots can only hold pre-`')'` text, because the lift and trailing blocks have not run yet), guarded in the compound arm so an outer paren level cannot **widen** a boundary an inner level claimed, and suppressing the lift-from-right block (which incidentally makes `(A LIMIT 2) UNION ALL (C ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 1)` correct). The planner consumes it by **not** clearing the sort/limit before planning the head branch, letting the recursive `planSelect` apply them below the `SetOp` — more faithful than re-resolving at set-op level, since a leaf branch may sort by a non-output expression (`ORDER BY x*-1`). No fold change is needed: a precedence barrier at segment 0 is vacuous. Also fixes a latent plan-cache hazard found in the same lines — the `InnerSegmentCount` path blanked `s.OrderBy`/`Limit`/`Offset` without restoring them, so a second `Plan()` of the same AST produced an unlimited plan; a `sortLimitConsumed` local replaces the mutation. Accepted BY VALUE against PG 18.3 (port 65438): 18 executor cases + 2 planner structural invariants + 7 parser AST pins, **proved to fail 8 executor subtests and both planner invariants at pre-fix `19d844b4`** while every control passed there. **TPC-DS cannot reach the defect** — a reflection walk over all 99 query files found zero `InnerSortLimit` nodes — and the SF0.5 set-op subset (Q23 Q38 Q49 Q87) came back checksum-identical to the HEAD sweep. Two PG behaviours stay deferred (an outer ORDER BY colliding with the head boundary; a trailing clause after the `')'` discarding the inner one), both with the same real fix: the chain must become a tree. |
| 0125-0018 | [A parenthesised set-op chain is a *query* operand, not an expression (M0125-0018)](0125-0018-setop-chain-as-query-operand.md) | accepted | The fourth member of 0125-0006's class, and the one with both a loud and a quiet half. `x IN ((A) EXCEPT (B))` and `EXISTS ((A) EXCEPT (B))` raised syntax errors; a probe found a **third** sibling the report never named, `x = ANY ((A) UNION (B))`; and the same root cause produced a silent variant — `x IN ((SELECT multirow))` parsed as a one-element VALUE LIST holding a scalar subquery and raised `21000 more than one row returned by a subquery` where PG simply answers the IN (`select 1 in ((select 1 union select 2))` = `t`). Root cause: `parseInTail`, `parseExistsExpr` and `parseAnyTail` each chose between gram.y's `in_expr: select_with_parens \| '(' expr_list ')'` (and `sub_type … select_with_parens \| … '(' a_expr ')'`; EXISTS has NO expression alternative) using **one token** of lookahead — "is the next token SELECT/VALUES?" — and `select_with_parens` nests, so every parenthesised chain begins with a `(` that fails the test. Peeling the `(` run is NOT sufficient either: `((select 1),(select 2))`, `((select 1)::int)` and `((select 1) + 1)` are all expressions in PG. The discriminator is **what follows the group's matching `)`** — a `,`/`::`/operator continues an expression; `)`, a set operator, `ORDER`, `LIMIT`, `OFFSET` or `FOR` continues a query. Fix = `selectWithParensAhead()` (non-consuming depth walk, so no backtracking machinery is needed — the parser has none) + `parseQueryOperandWithParens()` at all three sites, delegating to `parseParenthesisedSelectStmt`, which means the operand inherits 0125-0016's precedence and 0125-0017's head-branch sort/limit for free (asserted, not assumed). EXISTS stays strict: `EXISTS ((1))` is still a syntax error. Accepted BY VALUE against PG 18.3 (port 65438): 20 executor cases + 16 parser AST pins, **proved to fail 14 executor and 10 parser subtests at pre-fix `74f4b264`** while every control passed there. **TPC-DS cannot reach it** — zero of the 99 SF0.5 query files contain `(in\|exists\|any\|all)\s*\(\s*\(` — so this is parser hygiene for hand-written SQL and the regress corpus, not a round-2 blocker. Two ledger rows deferred: ANY/ALL still accepts an `expr_list` PG rejects, and `FETCH FIRST … ROWS ONLY` is unspellable anywhere in goopg (no `KwFetch` token). |
| 0125-0019 | [An aggregate's own ORDER BY decides its VALUE, and `string_agg` ignored it (M0125-0019)](0125-0019-aggregate-own-order-by.md) | accepted | `select string_agg(x::text, ',' order by x) from (values (3),(1),(2)) v(x)` returned `3,1,2` against PG's `1,2,3` — one row, one column, right type, wrong content: the same quiet wrong-answer class as M0125-0009/-0010 that a row-count gate is structurally blind to. PG's `ORDER BY` inside an aggregate is not presentational; `nodeAgg.c` tuplesorts the transition inputs and only then runs the transition function (`process_ordered_aggregate_single`/`_multi`), and PG *rejects* the clause where it would be presentational (`… ORDER BY … OVER ()` ⇒ `aggregate ORDER BY is not implemented for window functions`), so there is no window path to keep in sync. Root cause is a **sibling asymmetry inside one `switch`**: `applyAgg` has exactly two order-sensitive built-in branches, and `array_agg` captured its keys while its neighbour `string_agg` concatenated in arrival order. The clause was intact everywhere upstream — parser (`FuncCall.OrderBy`), M0125-0009's `funcCallTailKey`, and the planner (`AggregateCall.OrderBy`, with `NullsFirst` already defaulted by `sortByNullsFirst`). This also closes a **latent second defect**: `planner.AggregateIsOrderSensitive` already permitted a parallel plan under an ordered `string_agg` on the premise that "the aggregate sorts its own input" — false until now, so such a plan could shuffle differently on every run. Fix = deferred concatenation (`strElems`/`strDelims`/`strElemKeys`, used only when `len(OrderBy) > 0`, so the common path allocates nothing new) plus `aggOrderBySortedIdx`, one **stable** comparator now shared by both branches so they cannot diverge again. The subtle part is the delimiter: it is a per-row argument, PG appends the **right-hand** row's own delimiter and drops the first, so delimiters must ride the same permutation as the values (oracle-verified, not assumed: `string_agg(n, d order by n)` over `('c','|'),('a','+'),('b','*')` = `a*b|c`). Accepted BY VALUE against PG 18.3 (port 65438): 17 subtests covering ASC/DESC, non-argument and expression sort keys, two-key mixed direction, NULL keys under ASC-default/`NULLS FIRST`/DESC-default, NULL values, the per-row delimiter, `DISTINCT`, empty input, per-GROUP ordering, and `array_agg` as the shared-comparator control — **13 proved to fail at `6088e41b` while all three controls passed there**. **TPC-DS cannot reach it** — zero of the 100 query files use `string_agg`/`array_agg`/`json_agg`/`xmlagg`. Two ledger rows deferred: goopg holds a `'\xaa'::bytea` literal as six-character TEXT (`length`=6 vs 2, `encode` returns `''`), filed as M0125-0021, which is why the bytea test asserts order only; and `json_agg`/`jsonb_agg`/`xmlagg`/`json_object_agg`/`jsonb_object_agg` have no `applyAgg` branch at all. |
| 0125-0021 | [A `bytea` value, not escaped text (M0125-0021)](0125-0021-pg-faithful-bytea-value.md) | accepted | `'\xaabb'::bytea` was the six-character **string** `\xaabb`, not the two bytes `0xAA 0xBB`, and `encode()` was a stub returning `''` for every input. Two of the three symptoms are loud (`length('\xaabb'::bytea)`=6 vs PG 2; `order by b` sorted by the backslash); the third is not, and it is why this is a defect rather than a gap — `encode` is *the* way a caller hex-dumps a bytea, so returning `''` instead of `42883` made a hex dump silently produce nothing. Root cause: `evalCast` had **no `bytea` arm**, so a cast to that type name fell through the pass-through default and kept `KindString`; `encodeValuePG` had the same hole from the other side, so a bytea column stored whatever characters the datum carried. `KindBytes` already existed and `decode()` already produced it — what was missing was any path from a literal into it. Fix = `internal/executor/bytea.go`, transliterations of `byteain`/`hex_decode_safe`/`esc_decode`/`pg_base64_decode`/`hex_encode`/`esc_encode`/`pg_base64_encode`/`byteaout`, wired in **sibling pairs** (Hard-won Rule #2): cast ↔ storage encoder (both call `byteaIn`), `decode(…,'hex')` ↔ `'\x…'::bytea` (both call `hexDecodePG`), `<bytea>::text` ↔ the wire renderer, and executor result Kind ↔ planner `exprType`'s advertised column type — a `KindBytes` datum typed `text` reaches psql as raw bytes. The comparator arm is load-bearing, not cosmetic: once a column holds two bytes, `where b = '\xaabb'` would have matched **nothing**, converting a wrong number into a silently empty result set. Three upstream details are easy to get wrong and are pinned: `encode(…,'escape')` is `esc_encode` (NUL/high-bit/backslash only — a `0x0a` stays a raw newline), NOT `byteaout`'s escape mode; `pg_base64_encode` wraps at 76 characters so its own output must be decodable (Go's `base64.StdEncoding` rejects those newlines); and hex diagnostics are `22023` while `byteain`'s escape pass raises `22P02`. Also removed three pre-existing `decode()` deviations (it stripped a `\x` prefix PG rejects, passed invalid backslash sequences through, and rejected the newlines `encode()` emits). Accepted BY VALUE: a 27-statement matrix run through psql against a throwaway goopg server and against the PG 18.3 oracle (port 65438) diffed **byte-identical**, plus 40 by-value subtests asserting payload bytes, datum Kind, advertised column type and both SQLSTATE families. Three ledger rows deferred: `int → bytea` casts (PG 11's `int4send` route, `length(123::bytea)`=4), the `bytea_output = escape` GUC, and the remaining bytea operators (`position`/`overlay`/`trim`/`get_byte`/`set_byte`/`bit_length`). |
| 0125-0020 | [The set-op chain becomes a tree (M0125-0020)](0125-0020-setop-chain-as-tree.md) | accepted | The structural fix behind four deferral rows from M0125-0006/-0017: goopg stored a set-op chain as a **linked list** (`SelectStmt.SetOp.Right`) whose head doubled as its leftmost operand, so a parenthesised head branch and the whole compound were ONE node sharing ONE `OrderBy`/`Limit`/`Offset` slot. `parseParenthesisedSelectStmt` also absorbed a set-operator written AFTER the `')'` into the parenthesised query's own chain. Two PG behaviours were unreachable while that held — `(A ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 2) UNION ALL (C) ORDER BY 1 DESC` (PG `9,2,1`; goopg dropped the outer sort) and `((A ORDER BY 1 LIMIT 2) UNION ALL C) LIMIT 1` (the inner LIMIT was overwritten) — and a worktree probe at `8ce216dd` showed the damage was **wider than filed**: three further shapes returned wrong ROWS, not merely a wrong order (`… ORDER BY 1 DESC LIMIT 2` gave `9,3` for `9,2`; `((A LIMIT 1) UNION ALL (G LIMIT 1)) ORDER BY 1 DESC` gave a single row `3` for `2,1`). Three annotations existed only to describe the overlap — `ParenBranches` (M0125-0006), `InnerSegmentCount` (M0097-0044), `InnerSortLimit` (M0125-0017) — each correct for its own case and none able to express the combination. PG needs none: `select_with_parens` is a LEAF operand of `select_clause` (`gram.y`), so trailing text always attaches ABOVE the parenthesised query and `transformSetOperationStmt` (`analyze.c`) receives a proper tree. Fix = a **grouping node** (`SelectStmt.SetOpOperand`): when a set-operator or `ORDER`/`LIMIT`/`OFFSET` follows the `')'`, the parser gives the parenthesised branch its own SelectStmt and hangs the trailing clauses on a fresh node above it. Token *consumption* is unchanged — only where clauses are STORED — which is why the whole existing -0006/-0016/-0017 matrix stayed green unmodified. `Parenthesized` is sharpened to "nothing followed the `')'`", which keeps the lift-from-right-branch rule working. Retires `parenBoundary`, the paren-boundary half of `cutAt`, `headSortLimit`/`innerBoundary`/`sortLimitConsumed`, and all three annotations; `setOpBindsTighter` survives with `foldSetOpRange` as its only caller, where M0125-0016's precedence climb now handles `A UNION (B) INTERSECT (C)` uniformly instead of by special case. A grouping node has no target list, so the analyzer gained `setOpLeftmostBranch` (PG names a set operation's columns after its leftmost branch) at four sites, and eight structural walkers plus two simple-SELECT gates learned to descend through it. Accepted BY VALUE against PG 18.3: 13 new executor subtests **proved to fail 5 at `8ce216dd`** with every control green, plus a 27-statement `psql` matrix that is **byte-identical** to PG. Gates: units PASS, `tpch-spotcheck.sh` PASS (Q12=2, Q13=35), TPC-DS SF0.5 subset probe over the ten set-op queries PASS=6/MISMATCH=0 with **Q87 and Q23 — the only TPC-DS queries whose parse shape this alters — checksum-identical to the `sweep-20260729-123114` baseline**. Two pre-existing gaps deferred: `CREATE VIEW v AS (SELECT …) UNION …` is rejected by the view-body parser (identical at `8ce216dd`), and `catalog.renameColumnInSelect` still skips a set-op's right branch. |
| 0125-0024 | [Two expression-*identity* fail-opens that COLLIDE (M0125-0024)](0125-0024-expression-identity-collisions.md) | implemented | **EXECUTED 2026-07-30.** The M0125-0002 census's two worst members, and worst in KIND, not in arm count: both compute an identity, so an unenumerated type is not *skipped* but **conflated** — a traversal that fails open loses information, an identity function that fails open INVENTS it. `planExprContentKey` keyed aggregate STATE-SHARING with a `default:` of `fmt.Sprintf("%T", e)`, so any two distinct expressions of one unenumerated type shared a `SharedStateSlot`, and the executor's leader/follower copy (`operators_join_agg.go:1699-1760`) then made the second aggregate report the first's value — M0097-0032's shipped-wrong-answer shape. `*BinaryOp` was one of the 28 conflated types, so `ua(a + b)` and `ua(a - b)` collided: reachable from ordinary SQL, not a corner. `exprEqual`'s `%T%v` fallback was wrong in **both** directions at once — `%v` prints a NESTED pointer as an address (structurally equal expressions read unequal, i.e. a spurious `42P10` at `planner.go:1623`) and prints `pos` (the same literal at another offset read unequal), where PG's `equal()` excludes location outright (`COMPARE_LOCATION_FIELD` is a no-op in `equalfuncs.c`). Fix = one new primitive (`exprSelfKey`, the node's OWN identity-bearing fields, complete over all 32 types and gated with the other two switches in both directions) plus a fourth driver over `exprChildSlots` (`exprIdentityKey`). It returns a **decidability flag rather than a bool**, because the two callers translate "undecidable" in **opposite** directions and that asymmetry is the safety argument: an unkeyable node keys **per pointer** for state sharing (never share) and reads **not equal** for DISTINCT ON (a false negative is diagnosable; a false positive is not). Both functions lost their own type switches, so **both census pins are DELETED, not demoted** — RC-1a class 50 → 48, census 64 → 63. The `*ColumnRef` divergence nobody had noticed as a pair (`SourceTableIdx/Index` vs `Index`) resolves to **`Index` alone**: `SchemaColumn.SourceTableIdx` documents zero as "unknown / derived" (`plan.go:27-37`), so it is auxiliary disambiguation metadata with a hole rather than a `varno`, and both callers compare expressions resolved against the SAME coordinate space. Gates: every pin proved to FAIL at `da6d2c0c` and pass after — including the VALUE pin, where both `ua_sum(CASE …)` calls got `SharedStateSlot=0`; `TestExprIdentitySiblingsAgree` makes a future divergence a test failure; units PASS; `plan-diff LABEL=tpcds-round2-head MODE=structural` **22/22 MATCH** (the now-laxer `pathKeyEqual` moved no plan). Two ledger rows own what is left: the executor half of the value gate through a real `CREATE AGGREGATE`, and `exprIdentityKey` still ACCEPTING `scopeIgnore`, which for an identity question is a wrong-answer policy held off only by a comment and a test that asserts the two policies differ. **↳ THE EXECUTOR HALF IS NOW CLOSED (2026-07-30, §5.1) and it changed the verdict on this fix: both directions are USER-VISIBLE.** `internal/executor/agg_state_sharing_value_test.go` drives the leader/follower copy through a real `CREATE AGGREGATE` over a real plpgsql sfunc — no new fixture machinery was needed, because `executeSFuncCall` already falls back to `executeStoredRoutine` and `RAISE NOTICE` lands in `ctx.Notices`, so the test COUNTS sfunc invocations instead of inferring them (3 → 6 for two unshared calls over 3 rows). At `da6d2c0c` `SELECT ua_sum(a+b), ua_sum(a-b)` returned **`(77, 77)`** where PG returns `(77, -63)`: one row of plausible numbers with the second column silently echoing the first, which is precisely why no row-count gate in this programme could have seen it. The same file also discharges §4's UNMEASURED half against the oracle (PG 18.3 on 65438): `SELECT DISTINCT ON (CASE …) … ORDER BY CASE …` was **rejected** at `da6d2c0c` with `42P10 SELECT DISTINCT ON expressions must match initial ORDER BY expressions` — a statement PG accepts and answers with the three rows HEAD now returns — because `%T%v` printed the two structurally identical `*CaseExpr`s' nested pointers as addresses. So this was a **wrong-ERROR fix as well as a wrong-answer fix**, and the remaining ledger row is `scopeIgnore` alone. |
| 0125-0025 | [A raising aggregate support function must abort the statement (M0125-0025)](0125-0025-sfunc-error-propagation.md) | implemented | **EXECUTED 2026-07-30.** M0125-0024's third ledger row claimed a code path rather than an observed wrong answer; it is an observed wrong answer. A user-defined aggregate whose `SFUNC`, `COMBINEFUNC` or `FINALFUNC` **raised** had its error discarded and the query answered anyway — measured at `0de1b404`, `SELECT p_rsum(a) FROM raise_t` returned **`1`** (the sum of the rows transitioned *before* the raise) where PG 18.3 aborts with `ERROR: boom 2`; the shared-DISTINCT-slot form returned `(1, 1)`; a raising `FINALFUNC` returned `NULL`; a raising `COMBINEFUNC` returned the un-combined partial state `6`. A plausible value of the right type in a result set of the right shape — M0125-0024's class exactly, and structurally invisible to every row-count gate in this programme. **Two independent swallows**, which is why it survived: `executeSFuncCall` discarded each candidate routine's error (`_ = rerr`, twice) and synthesised `42883 aggregate state function "x" does not exist`, so a routine that was PRESENT and FAILED was reported as MISSING — and that misreporting is what hid the second swallow, since a caller inspecting the error saw a lookup failure, not a user error. Then all seven call sites read `if serr == nil { state = newState }`, i.e. *on failure keep the previous state*; the three transition loops (`applyAgg`, `finishAgg`'s DISTINCT/ORDER BY dedup, and `Open`'s leader/follower pre-compute — the site -0024's row called the worst) are separate code and each swallowed independently. PG has no such branch to write: `advance_transition_function` (`postgres/src/backend/executor/nodeAgg.c`) invokes the sfunc through `FunctionCallInvoke`, so an `ereport(ERROR)` unwinds the statement with the routine's own SQLSTATE. **A blanket propagate would have been wrong**, which is the design's one real decision: `executeSFuncCall` doubles as the lookup for the built-in transition functions it models inline and is called speculatively for slots an aggregate never declared, so its `42883` is a NORMAL outcome — an aggregate with no `FINALFUNC` finishes on its state alone. The two failure modes therefore had to become *decidable* and propagate in OPPOSITE directions (the same shape -0024's `exprIdentityKey` needed): `errSFuncNotFound` → swallow, `sfuncRaised(err)` → propagate. It unwraps to its `*ExecError` so `errors.As` still reaches the 42883. A second subtlety: candidates are matched by **arity, not signature**, so several may be tried where PG resolves one — the fix keeps trying after a failure and remembers the FIRST error, changing only the all-failed outcome, so every call that succeeds today still succeeds by the same route. `finishAgg` needed an error channel and had ~103 `return <Datum>` statements of which only the leading `if call.UserAgg != nil` branch can fail, so its built-in tail was lifted verbatim into `finishBuiltinAgg` — no re-indentation, no touched returns — which also documents that built-in finalization cannot fail. Gates: 7 new subtests, every `want` MEASURED against PG 18.3 on port 65438 inside a rolled-back transaction (the reference DB left byte-unchanged, verified); goopg's `RAISE EXCEPTION` is `P0001` like PG's, so the fixed paths reproduce the oracle's errors identically (`P0001: boom 2`, `P0001: final boom 6`); `TestMissingSFuncStillFallsThrough` pins the half that must NOT change; executor + units suites PASS. **Two gaps found and deferred with ledger rows**, one of them by the gate itself: the two `windowOp` sites are now plumbed but **unreachable**, because the v0 analyzer rejects a user-defined aggregate in `OVER (...)` with `0A000` before the executor is involved (PG accepts it), so that test asserts the durable invariant rather than a message; and `applyAgg`'s neighbouring `evalExprSlot` calls for `Arg2`/`ExtraArgs` swallow in exactly the same shape, dropping a failed argument and calling the sfunc with FEWER arguments than declared. |
| root-0032 | [Crash restart must not leave the cluster unstartable: WAL stream anchoring and end-of-WAL](root-0032-crash-restart-wal-stream-anchoring.md) | accepted | M-NIGHTLY triage found the surviving `regress/{portals_p2,select,select_distinct}` "divergences" were never measured: after `misc` timed out, root-0029's recovery restart FAILED (`goopg: wal replay: decode at offset 771751920: invalid record header: unknown rmid=31`) and 53 consecutive cases reported a phantom `deferred:`. Root cause is not the regress suite at all — **goopg could not start after a crash** once retention had run, reproduced with `pgbench -c 16` + `kill -9` at ~570 MB of WAL. Three defects, one theme (both scanners assumed the stream begins on a record boundary and stays valid to the end): (1) a hole in `pg_wal` — the normal residue of a SIGKILL during `removeOldSegments`, which walks obsolete segments newest-first and so leaves the OLDEST behind — was fatal (`wal: gap at segment N`); the live stream is now the longest contiguous run ending at the highest segment (`liveSegmentRunStart`, shared by replay and `detectWritePos`), safe because only retention makes holes and retention only removes below the checkpoint keep point. (2) A segment opening with `XLP_FIRST_IS_CONTRECORD` had its continuation bytes decoded as a record header, so `scanLastSegmentEnd` reported the segment as empty and a reopened writer appended OVER durable records — 54–97 records destroyed per reopen in the negative control, on clean reopens too, and the source of the stale bytes a later crash restart reads as `unknown rmid=N`; both scanners now skip `MAXALIGN(xlp_rem_len)` as upstream's `xlogreader.c` does. (3) An unreadable tail (concurrent appenders + SIGKILL leaves 8 bytes of a record header durable with no contrecord flag on the next page — dumped from the preserved directory) was returned as an error instead of ending redo; `readAllPageAware` now stops and logs (`endOfWAL`), matching `report_invalid_record`/`ReadRecord`. Tests: `TestSegmentGapFromInterruptedRetention`, `TestReopenAfterSegmentStraddlingRecord` (fails if no payload size exercises the straddle), `TestLiveSegmentRunStart`; `TestDetectWritePos_GapDetectionAfterNonZeroStart` inverted — its old contract WAS the bug. STILL OPEN (ledger, §5): with the read side fixed the same reproduction now fails one stage later in redo (`heap-update add new tuple: not enough free space in page`), and the regress harness still emits one phantom `deferred:` per case after a failed restart. Gates: `go test ./internal/wal/ ./internal/initdb/ ./internal/storage/` PASS; negative control on both halves; `RALPH_PRECOMMIT_SCOPE=units scripts/ralph-precommit-test.sh` PASS. |
| root-0033 | [Redo of a redirect-only page prune must compact the page](root-0033-redo-prune-redirect-only-compaction.md) | accepted | Closes root-0032 §5: with the WAL *read* path fixed, the same crash reproduction (`analysis/wal-crash-restart-repro.sh`, `pgbench -c 16` + `kill -9` at ~580 MB of WAL) still left the cluster unstartable, now failing inside redo with `xlog heap-update add new tuple: storage: not enough free space in page`. The failing record is 79 bytes — an incremental update — so redo had to apply it onto a page reconstructed from earlier records, and that reconstruction had **less** free space than the running server's page. Cause: goopg's single runtime pruner `pagePruneCore` (`internal/storage/prune.go`) compacts on BOTH arms — with the dead set when slots became unused, and with a nil dead set when the prune produced only redirects, because `VacuumHeapPageBySlots` repacks only `ItemIDNormal` survivors and a just-redirected chain root is `ItemIDRedirect`, so its tuple body is reclaimed. The PG-format redo arm `replayDecodedXLogHeapPrune` (introduced by the A7 `EncodeHeapPruneOptPG` switch) guarded that repack on `len(unused) > 0`, so a **redirect-only** prune — the common shape in a pgbench HOT workload, where a two-link chain has a dead root and a live tip and no dead intermediates — set the redirects, cleared `pd_prune_xid` and skipped the compaction, permanently shrinking the replayed page's free space. The legacy native arm `replayHeapPruneOpt` in the same file has always compacted unconditionally, so only the PG-format sibling had drifted (Hard-won Rule #2). Fix: compact whenever the record carries any prune action (`len(redirects) > 0 \|\| len(unused) > 0`), matching `pagePruneCore`'s condition and upstream's `heap_xlog_prune_freeze` → `heap_page_prune_execute` → `PageRepairFragmentation`; deliberately not unconditional, since goopg emits freeze as its own `xl_heap_prune` and the runtime freeze path does not compact. Verified end-to-end (identical repro: HEAD fails, fixed build reports `RESTART_OK`) and by a non-vacuous `TestReplayPGHeapPruneRedirectOnlyCompactsLikeRuntime`, which asserts the replayed page is byte-identical to the runtime-pruned page apart from `pd_lsn` (negative control: `pd_upper` 8112 vs 8160). |
| root-0035 | [Startup replay must use the cluster's `wal_segment_size`, not 16 MiB](root-0035-wal-segment-size-derived-from-stream.md) | accepted | Closes the pass-required `TestRestartAfterRetention` (`internal/server`), red since root-0032. The tell is in the error itself: replay reported `record 0 lsn[301990201,301990520]` on a cluster whose checkpoints sat at `17207361`/`18882449` — the same segment number (18), multiplied by `DefaultSegmentSize` (16 MiB) instead of the cluster's actual 1 MiB. `readAllUncached` anchors the decoded stream at `baseOffset = firstSegNo * segmentSize`, and all three recovery entry points (`initdb.Open` → `ReplayFromDirWithMgr(mgr, pg_wal, 0)`, the ~30 catalog-recovery modules' `ReadAll(walDir, 0)`, and `DiscoverLastCheckpointLSN`) resolved `0` to 16 MiB — nothing on that path ever learned the cluster's size, since `OpenOptions.WALSegmentSize` fed only the *writer* config. LSNs 16× too large **disarm redo's `pd_lsn` idempotency check**: no page ever looks up-to-date, startup re-applied already-applied inserts, and the page overflowed with `xlog heap-insert apply: not enough free space in page` — an unstartable cluster. The bug predates root-0032, which merely made the path reachable: before its `XLP_FIRST_IS_CONTRECORD` skip, the leading continuation bytes decoded as garbage and the walk yielded zero records, so the wrong base was never used. Fix takes the size from the stream the way upstream's context-free readers do — `pg_waldump`'s `search_directory()` reads `longhdr->xlp_seg_size` and validates it with `IsValidWalSegSize` — via `detectSegmentSizeAt` (the live run's first segment always carries a long page header whose `SegSize` `buildPageHeader` writes from the writer's config), resolving caller-supplied → detected → default; `ReplayFromDirWithMgr`/`DiscoverLastCheckpointLSN` stop pre-coercing `0`. No signature changed, so every 0-passing caller is fixed together and keeps sharing the `segmentSize == 0` recovery memoization an explicit-plumbing fix would have bypassed; a default 16 MiB cluster is byte-for-byte unaffected. Non-vacuous `TestReadAllDerivesSegmentSizeFromStream` (detection stubbed out ⇒ 1921 vs 3000 records) + `TestIsValidWalSegSize`. Deferred (ledger): `initdb.WriteBootstrapWAL` still hardcodes 16 MiB because `initdb.Init` has no segment-size option, so a fresh non-default cluster reads 16 MiB until the bootstrap segment ages out. |
| root-0034 | [`float` is a grammar-level alias, not a type name: the opt_float reduction](root-0034-float-type-alias-opt-float-reduction.md) | accepted | Closes the last M-NIGHTLY `regress/index_including` divergence, and it was not the index-only scan over a `name` key the case's title advertises. §10's fixture is `CREATE TABLE nametbl (c1 int, c2 name, c3 float)`, and the row was gone from a plain seq scan on a table with no index at all: goopg's parser stored the literal token `float`, which has no `pg_type` entry (PostgreSQL resolves `FLOAT [ (p) ]` entirely inside the grammar, `gram.y` opt_float — no precision → float8, 1..24 → float4, 25..53 → float8, outside → ERROR 22023, and the reduction is a *rename* so the precision never becomes a typmod). The token therefore reached `catalog.TypeNameToOID`'s `default: return OIDText` fallback and the column was created as **text** (atttypid 25, attlen -1), while `internal/executor`'s own independent type tables (`codec.go:482`, `expr.go:3035`) list `"float"` next to float8 and encoded an 8-byte IEEE-754 datum — Hard-won Rule #2 in its encode↔decode form, failing silently and totally: `INSERT 0 1` followed by zero rows forever (negative control renders the column as `"-DT\xfb!\t@"`, the LE float64 bytes handed to a text decoder). Fix performs PG's reduction where PG performs it: `normalizeFloatTypeName` implements opt_float verbatim and is wired into the four type-name sites that can carry a typmod (`parseColumnType` — which also covers PL/pgSQL DECLARE via `parseTypeRef` — `parseCreateDomain`, `parseCastTail`, `parseCastFuncExpr`), each skipping quoted/schema-qualified names since PG reaches opt_float only from the FLOAT_P keyword. `catalog.TypeNameToOID` is deliberately NOT given a `float` arm — upstream's `typenameTypeId` cannot resolve it either. opt_float's rejections are 22023, not 42601, so `parser.SyntaxError` gained an optional `Code` and the server's three parse-error sites route through a new `syntaxErrorCode`; message, caret and SQLSTATE are byte-identical to PG. Also fixed in passing: `CREATE DOMAIN d AS float` (was typbasetype=text) and `x::float(24)` (was double precision, PG gives real). Verified by a parser table test, a non-vacuous end-to-end executor round-trip on the §10 fixture, and `TestPort_RegressSuite/index_including` PASSING in full-suite ordering (88-case prefix, 244 s). |
| root-0036 | [`SELECT DISTINCT` silently discarded its own `ORDER BY` direction](root-0036-select-distinct-order-by-direction.md) | accepted | Closes M-NIGHTLY item (e)'s `regress/select_distinct`. The `USING >` and the `person*` inheritance scan in the failing query are both red herrings — reduced, the bug is that `SELECT DISTINCT p.age FROM person p ORDER BY age DESC` answers in **ascending** order while the unqualified `SELECT DISTINCT age FROM person ORDER BY age DESC` is correct. goopg does not plan DISTINCT the PG way (upstream builds the distinct clause FROM the sort clause — `transformDistinctClause`, `parse_clause.c` — so `Unique` sits over a path already sorted by those pathkeys and dedup and ordering are one operation); instead `distinctOp` re-sorts ascending to make duplicates adjacent and an outer Sort re-applies the user's `ORDER BY` (M0097-0046). That outer Sort was the ONLY carrier of direction, and it was dropped whenever its key failed to resolve — which two facts made the common case: `resolveOrderBySubstitution` rewrites a bare `ORDER BY` name into the matching target's OWN expression (so `age` becomes the qualified `p.age`), and the outer context is schema-only with no range bindings while `SchemaColumn` carries no table name at all. No error, no warning — `distinctOp`'s ascending sort just becomes the answer. Same mechanism swallowed every computed target (`p.age+1`), and a star target failed differently (substitution deliberately skips `StarExpr`, leaving an `IntegerConst` the outer arm had no positional path for): 7 of 8 measured shapes were wrong, only the unqualified one — the shape hand-written test SQL uses — worked. Fix keeps the design and makes resolution succeed, in three arms: positional against the Distinct output BEFORE substitution (mirroring the normal ORDER BY path's own `IntegerConst` arm), then the pre-existing schema-only `resolveExpr`, then new `distinctSortKeyOutputIndex` — resolve against whichever surface built the targets (window/aggregate/pre-projection ctx) and structurally match against `proj.Targets` with `exprEqual`, whose index IS the output column. Sound because PG rejects any SELECT DISTINCT whose ORDER BY key is absent from the select list with 42P10, so a legal key always occupies a select-list position; this also makes DISTINCT and DISTINCT ON agree on how a key is located. Non-vacuous `TestDistinctHonoursOrderByDirection` (10 subtests, all `want` values captured from PG 18.3 on :65438; 7 fail with the hunk stashed); `TestPort_RegressSuite/select_distinct` SKIP → PASS (and unlike its `errors`/`portals_p2`/`select` siblings it DOES reproduce in isolation, giving a 1.6 s repro loop). Gates: planner+executor, units, `internal/server` (explicitly — the units gate misses it), `tpch-spotcheck.sh` (Q12=2, Q13=35). TPC-DS scoped by inspection instead of the ~1 h sweep: only Q41 of 100 has a DISTINCT that also carries ORDER BY, and Q41/Q6/Q87 match the oracle and the 2026-07-27 baseline exactly. Deferred (3 ledger rows): DISTINCT still does not adopt the query's sort operators; `ORDER BY … USING <op>` infers direction from the operator's NAME (`sortUsingIsDesc`) rather than a btree opclass strategy (`get_ordering_op_properties`); and both the SF0.5 and tpch-spotcheck gates are row-count-only, so this entire wrong-order/right-rows class is invisible to them. |
| root-0037 | [The nightly held a 16-core host for 6h45m after its sweep had finished](root-0037-nightly-server-shutdown-ladder.md) | accepted | Nightly `20260729-002344` finished its TPC-H sweep at 02:07:15 and was still holding the host at 08:50, with no error in any log — the stage log ends on `sweep done`, the server log on a **successful** `shutdown checkpoint complete`. Cause: two queries hit the 1200 s per-query cap; killing psql kills only the client, and differencing `connection established` against `connection closed` pids leaves **exactly one** survivor — the Q13 backend `pid=40`, which logged `client connection lost mid-query; cancelling statement` (`internal/server/eof_watch.go:113`) and never finished. `goopg stop` then took its checkpoint, cancelled the run context and drained the accept loop (65434 was gone from `ss` while the process lived), but graceful shutdown cannot return until every backend has, so the process never exited and `stage-tpch.sh`'s **untimed** `wait ${server_pid}` inherited the hang — parking the run before its TPC-DS stage, pinning 7.5 GiB and the run lock, and (via the new host-quiet guards) blocking the next day's M0124 measurements too. Fix: `stop_goopg_server` in `ci/batch/lib/common.sh` — a bounded ladder `graceful(120s) → -mode immediate(60s) → SIGTERM(30s) → SIGKILL`, 210 s worst case, used by both `stage-tpch.sh` and `stage-tpcds.sh` (which carried the identical two lines; `stage-pgbench.sh` already hard-killed). Two load-bearing details: liveness is read from process **state** (`ps -o stat=`, `Z*` = gone) because a background child answers `kill -0` while a zombie and the graceful rung would otherwise falsely time out on every healthy run; and `STOP_RUNG` is a global because `$(...)` would run the helper in a subshell where `wait` cannot reap the caller's child. The graceful rung missing its budget is the last moment the server exists to be inspected, so it now first pulls a goroutine dump — this loop could not, because goopg's pprof binds `127.0.0.1:6060` unconditionally and losing that race is logged only at `Debug`, so the nightly server had silently skipped it; both stages now pass a private `GOOPG_PPROF_ADDR`. Guarded by `ci/batch/lib/test_stop_ladder.sh` (all five rungs bounded + dump capture, ~50 s, no goopg build). The engine leak itself — a backend that ignores cancellation and blocks graceful shutdown forever, where PG's `pg_ctl stop -m fast` SIGTERMs each backend and `ProcessInterrupts` honours it — is NOT fixed here: it is an open M-NIGHTLY task + ledger row, and a sharper instance of root-0029's still-open orphaned-backend row. |
| root-0038 | [`ORDER BY … FOR UPDATE` over a join silently took no row lock](root-0038-lockrows-sort-over-join-ctid.md) | accepted | Found during M-NIGHTLY triage of `TestPort_IsolationEvalPlanQual` (AI-20260806-011323-001) — a **distinct** defect, and the nightly item stays open (§5). `SELECT a.*, FROM a, s WHERE a.k=s.k ORDER BY a.k FOR UPDATE OF a` returned the stale pre-update row in 4 ms without blocking, where PG blocks and returns the updated one: `FOR UPDATE` was a silent no-op, no tuple lock and no EvalPlanQual recheck. Drop the `ORDER BY` and the same query is correct (blocks 6005 ms → 1050); a single-relation `ORDER BY … FOR UPDATE` is correct too. Cause: goopg has no resjunk-`ctid` column (PG's `preprocess_targetlist` adds one per rowmark and `nodeLockRows.c` reads it back, so plan shape is irrelevant to locking there) and instead **reconstructs** the TID two ways — `lockRowsOp.scan` found by walking the operator tree, else the `MaterializedSlot.hasCTID` side-channel. Route 1 cannot work under a Sort and both walkers correctly return nil at a `sortOp` (after the sort has drained and reordered, the scan cursor points at an arbitrary tuple); route 2 is exactly the cover for that case (`sortOp.ctids`, M0118-0003) but only fires if the slot ENTERING the sort already has `hasCTID`. `seqScanOp` stamps it itself — hence the working single-relation case — but a `joinOp` forwards it only when `preserveCTIDRel` is set, and `markJoinPreserveCTID` recursed through Project/Filter/Join only, stopping dead at the Sort. Both routes empty ⇒ `drainAndStamp` found no TID ⇒ unlocked pass-through. Fix is one arm (`case *sortOp: markJoinPreserveCTID(v.child, targetRel)`); the walkers are deliberately left alone. A/B on two binaries differing only in that arm, identical plan shape both sides: 4 ms/600/no-block → 4008 ms/1050/blocked. Guard `TestPort_LockRowsSortOverJoinTakesRowLock` (`sort_over_join` + `join_no_sort` control), verified non-vacuous — with the arm removed only the former fails. Deferred (ledger): `sortOp` still drops the side-channel once it spills (`ctidsDisabled`), so a row-locking query whose sort exceeds `work_mem` loses the lock silently; and the walkers' switch knows 8 of ~70 operator types, so any other operator landing between `LockRows` and its scan leaves degrades to "no lock" the same silent way. |
| root-0039 | [`missing FROM-clause entry` swallowed the alias diagnosis](root-0039-error-missing-rte-alias-hint.md) | accepted | Closes the last deterministic blocker of M0127's S7 nightly gate — `regress/delete` (AI-20260806-011323-016), open since the 20260806 triage with `errorMissingRTE()` named as its resume point. Upstream `delete.sql` is one statement: `DELETE FROM delete_test dt WHERE delete_test.a > 25` must raise `invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "delete_test"` + `HINT: Perhaps you meant to reference the table alias "dt".`; goopg raised the bald `missing FROM-clause entry` with no hint. The ledger scoped this to DELETE — it was never about DELETE: **all five** shapes upstream distinguishes gave the identical wrong text (`delete.out`, `update.out`, `returning.out`, `insert_conflict.out`, and plain `SELECT t.a`/`t.*` over an aliased FROM entry). The missing piece is a *diagnosis*, not wording: `errorMissingRTE()` (`parse_relation.c`) looks the refname up a **second time ignoring aliases** (`searchRangeTableForRel`) and, on a hit, reports "you wrote the table's own name where only its alias is visible" instead of "the relation is absent". goopg did the first lookup and stopped, collapsing *renamed* and *absent* into one outcome. The pre-existing `blockOriginalName` machinery (M0097-0003) produced the right text but only at the two sites that SET the flag — and `analyzeDelete` was not one, so the analyzer's bald error pre-empted the planner's correct one; fixing that single call site would have turned `delete` green while leaving the other four wrong. One helper per resolver instead (`analyzer.errorMissingRTE` / `planner.errorMissingRTEPlan`), each walking its own lexical chain, skipping `qualifiedOnly` rels (ON CONFLICT's `excluded` is a keyword, not a user rename) and entries aliased to their own name (upstream's `strcmp(aliasname, relname) != 0` guard). **Both twins moved**: RETURNING scopes are built after analysis, so `RETURNING t.*` is served only by the planner. Also corrects 42712 (`duplicate_alias`) → **42P01** at the two `blockOriginalName` sites — upstream raises every branch with `ERRCODE_UNDEFINED_TABLE`; invisible in regress output, which is how it survived. `TestPort_RegressSuite/delete` SKIP→PASS, proven by A/B on builds differing only in these two files (`insert_conflict`/`returning`/`subselect`/`update` SKIP on both sides — deferred for unrelated reasons, not regressed). Guards `TestAnalyzeErrorMissingRTEAliasHint` + `TestPlanErrorMissingRTEAliasHint`, both verified non-vacuous. Deferred (ledger): upstream's middle branch — an entry that exists but is not visible from this part of the query, with its `errdetail` and LATERAL hint — needs a present-but-invisible notion goopg's scope chain does not have. |
| root-0040 | [The regress-suite wedge was a page latch stranded by a recovered panic](root-0040-btree-stranded-latch-release.md) | accepted | Names the M-NIGHTLY `regress/suite-wedge` root cause, open across nine loops and blocking M0127's S7 gate ("S5-ON survives a clean nightly cycle"). Evidence was a live specimen, not inference: an orphaned regress-suite server, data dir already deleted, whose goroutine dump showed the **checkpointer blocked ten minutes** on one slot's shared content latch (`flushBatch` ← `FlushAll` ← `runCheckpoint`) that **no live goroutine held** — and whose own log, at the same minute, recorded a recovered backend panic `storage: not enough free space in page` in `insertItemSorted` ← `insertIntoBlock` ← `Insert` ← `maintainUniqueIndexesForInsert`. `insertIntoBlock` takes the leaf's exclusive latch via `pinW` and releases it with an explicit `unpinW` (not a `defer` — the split path hands latches between frames), so a panic unwinding that window strands the latch forever, because `internal/server`'s per-connection `recover()` throws the owning goroutine away. Every part of the signature follows: a statement hangs past its own 5 s `statement_timeout` (a mutex wait observes no deadline — the item's hypothesis (b), now explained); the server stays fast otherwise (only that page is poisoned); the wedge case MOVES run to run (whoever next touches the page); and the shutdown checkpoint's `FlushAll` wants the same latch, so the server ignores SIGTERM — that is the orphaned-test-server crawl, same defect. PG cannot reach this state: `elog(ERROR)` longjmps and `AbortTransaction()` calls `LWLockReleaseAll()`; goopg has no equivalent. Fix is a local idempotent `wlatch` holder — `defer held.release()` covers the panic path while the eleven normal exits keep releasing explicitly. A first cut that kept a registry on the `*BTree` and swept it at each entry point was FALSIFIED by the package's own tests: `*BTree` is not goroutine-private (`TestConcurrentSearchAfterInserts` deadlocked) and callers latch outside any entry point (`lpdead_kill_test.go:225` double-released); a per-goroutine registry would need a goid on the descent hot path, which this repo has already paid for twice. Guards `TestStrandedLatchReleasedOnPanic` (non-vacuous — removing only the defer makes it HANG, the wedge in miniature) + `TestWlatchReleaseIsIdempotent`. Deferred (2 ledger rows): the trigger itself — `pageHasSpaceFor` says the item fits and `insertItemSorted` then panics that it does not — and the general gap at the descent's shared latches, the split path's locked-return slots, and every non-btree `Slot.Lock()` site in `internal/executor`. |
| root-0041 | [A partial index was selectable for quals its predicate never implied](root-0041-partial-index-predicate-guard.md) | accepted | The two survivors of nightly `20260806-232940` — `regress/portals_p2` and `regress/select`, the last items between the tree and M0127's S7 gate — were one wrong-answer bug, not the "output normalization" their label claimed. goopg chose partial indexes without proving the index predicate from the query quals, so a partial index silently returned **zero rows** for anything outside it: `onek2 WHERE unique1 = 50` took `Index Only Scan using onek2_u1_prtl` (predicate `unique1 < 20 OR unique1 > 980`) and returned 0 where 1 row exists. Both cases pass STANDALONE and fail in-suite — which had stalled three earlier loops as "does not reproduce" — because `onek2`'s partial indexes are created by `create_index`, so only a full-suite pass has them; the order dependence was the symptom, the missing guard the cause. PG proves the predicate in `check_index_predicates()` (`predicate_implied_by()` → `index->predOK`) and `create_index_paths()` skips an unproven index. goopg had already reached that conclusion in ONE place — `addOneOrderedIndexPath` declines `HasPredicate` with a comment saying why — but never mirrored it onto the main scan path, where `HasPredicate` had zero readers: the recurring sibling-path failure, with the guarded twin's green tests saying nothing about the exposed one. Fix mirrors the rule at `findBTreeIndexForColumn` (covering the plain path and all three `mhj_input_rewrite.go` sites) and `pickIndexCoveringAllLeadingColumns` (the parameterized path), using `continue` not `return nil` so a plain index on the same column still wins. Guards: `TestPartialIndexNotChosenForUnprovenQual` (non-vacuous — neutering both guards fails it), plus a still-chosen and a preferred-over-partial control so the fix cannot pass by disabling index scans. Verified in real suite order (89 → 87 diverging cases; `hash_index` recovered too), units + `tpch-spotcheck` (Q12=2, Q13=35). Deferred (3 ledger rows): port the implication prover so the index can be USED when implied; `regress/truncate` is independently nondeterministic (FK `DETAIL` ordering, 1 of 3 runs); and the nightly never sets `GOOPG_REGRESS_DIFF_DIR`, which is why this survived three loops unactionable. |
| 0125-0011 | [Merge join dropped every ON conjunct after the first (M0125-0011)](0125-0011-full-outer-join-on-conjunct-drop.md) | accepted | `runMergeJoin` joined on the single merge key and **never read `Join.Predicate`** — so every conjunct after the first, which is all `splitEqualityForHash` returns, was silently dropped at execution time. goopg routes RIGHT and FULL joins to `JoinAlgoMerge`, so both produced a **cross product inside each equal-key group** *and* lost rows: the pre-existing `cmp<0`/`cmp>0` arms only null-extend rows whose KEY found no partner, so a row whose key matched but whose residual failed could not be emitted at all. TPC-DS Q97's two-key FULL OUTER JOIN returned `2131274` — precisely its single-key count — where PG returns `836302` (= 548694+287769−161, the full-outer identity, which independently confirms the reference side). The fourth sibling-path instance of Hard-won Rule #2: nested-loop, lateral and hash all call `joinPredicateMatch`; only the merge twin omitted it, which is why the INNER probe was already right. Fix mirrors `nodeMergejoin.c` — `EXEC_MJ_JOINTUPLES` runs `ExecQual(joinqual)` per candidate pair inside the group, and `MJ_FILL_OUTER`/`MJ_FILL_INNER` null-extend what the joinqual rejected — so the group now evaluates the full predicate per pair, tracks `leftMatched`/`rightMatched`, and null-extends the residual-rejected rows by join type. Costs no allocation (`concatRows` already ran per pair; rejected pairs now skip their `append`). Verified as a 24-cell differential vs PG 18.3 (4 join types × 6 ON shapes, over duplicate keys, NULL join keys and NULL residual columns — all 24 match), a unit regression whose expected sets are the *measured* PG answers and which fails on all 5 subtests pre-fix, and TPC-DS Q97 at SF=1 = `541140|286927|161` with the full 5-row probe matrix matching. The **SF0.5 gate does see it**: the full 99-query sweep moved `PASS=73 CKMISMATCH=5` -> `PASS=74 CKMISMATCH=4` with **Q97 `CKMISMATCH -> PASS` as the only per-query change**, and a same-harness A/B reads pre-fix `ck=5687f61d9fdd4f93` vs post-fix `ck=65725195ebe13a3b` (the oracle) — so no anchor re-pinning is needed. **Also records the gate-integrity trap that nearly inverted that conclusion:** `scripts/tpcds-sf05-regression.sh`'s sweep path **never rebuilds `tmp/goopg-bench-bin`** (line 256 guards the build with `[[ -x … ]] ||` and lives in `load-goopg`, not `sweep`), so an earlier stash-and-re-sweep probe silently re-measured a stale binary and appeared to prove the gate blind. A source-level A/B against this gate is meaningless without an explicit `go build -o tmp/goopg-bench-bin ./cmd/goopg` per arm, and a green sweep after an edit does not prove the edit was exercised — `bench/tpcds/server.sh` rebuilds unconditionally, so which entry point started the server decides whether a change is under test at all. Deferred: `Join` still carries ONE key pair against PG's mergeclause *list*, so multi-key merge joins are now correct but less selective than PG (group on one column, filter the rest per pair). **Updated 2026-07-30 — the gate-integrity half is CLOSED, in D4a's format rather than a second ad-hoc one:** the sweep now builds unconditionally (`sf05_ensure_bin`, `SF05_NO_BUILD=1` to opt out, and the report then says its binary's provenance is unknown), prints the SF=1 harness's three fields verbatim (`# goopg:` / `# engine-id:` / `# engine-binary: running=… on-disk=…`), and **cannot swap engines silently across a restart** — `RESTART_AFTER_TIMEOUT` and the crash-restart re-exec `${GOOPG_BIN}` as it is *then*, so `sf05_guard_engine_stable` writes `*** SWEEP VOID: engine source changed mid-sweep ***` into the report when `engine-id` moves, and the benign docs/tracker-rebuild note when only the image does (D4a's measured false positive, preserved). The three definitions moved to `bench/tpcds/env_tpcds.sh` and `scripts/tpcds-bench-compare.sh` delegates to them, because the copy of a provenance rule that drifts is the one that stops catching the trap. Two guards ride along on the shared-path hazard that created it: rebuilding `tmp/goopg-bench-bin` is REFUSED while `ci/batch`/the SF=1 harness runs from it (`FORCE=1` does not waive this — it waives timing contamination, a different question), and `GOOPG_BIN` is env-overridable so a loop can build its own image. |
| 0125-0012 | [TPC-DS Q8: a `ColumnRef` below a FROM-subquery `Project` keeps its outer-scope index (M0125-0012)](0125-0012-q8-subquery-scope-index-remap.md) | accepted | Files the last round-1 error that never had an owning task. Q8 is the **only unresolved member of round 1's nine goopg-only errors** and one of just two `ERROR` cells in the complete SF=1 sweep (`ERROR 26 s`: `column ref ca_zip/57 out of MaterializedSlot range 1`; the server survives, so it is contained, not a crash). Records what already landed so it is not re-attempted: `9ddbc679`'s `containsSetOp` guard protected `pushdown.go:241`/`:264` and `planner.go:2078` but **never the remap path**, which is why Q8 kept failing after it; `9740fce9` then gave `buildBindingsPosMap` its `SetOp`/`RecursiveUnion`/`WorkTableScan`/`WindowAgg`/`ProjectSet`/`OrdinalityWrap`/`RowsFrom`/`IndexOnlyScan` arms plus a decline-on-unknown `default:`, and bounds-checked `*MaterializedSlot`/`*Slot` in `evalExprSlot` — that pair converted a backend-killing panic into a contained `XX000`. The residual is a **second coordinate space**: `ca_zip` = 57 is a global FROM-order index reaching a 1-column `MaterializedSlot` (the INTERSECT-in-FROM subquery's own `Project` scope, which `buildBindingsPosMap` never governs), and `remapSubqueryColumnRefs` rewrites only `Project` **targets**, leaving a `ColumnRef` inside a `Filter` below that `Project` holding the outer index. Design extends the pass to `Filter.Predicate`, `Join.LeftKey/RightKey` and `Aggregate.GroupExprs/Aggs` — **while preserving M0125-0010's verify-then-repair narrowing**, since a name-only search on the new arms would be the fourth *recurrence* of "ambiguous key resolved by taking the first match" (the fifth instance — `2e09250b` called M0125-0010 the "Third recurrence"), and prefers routing them through M0125-0001's driver over hand-rolling a fifth walker. Carries the acceptance trap that makes this defect unusual: **PG returns 0 rows for Q8 at SF=1**, so "goopg returns 0 rows" is satisfiable by any bug that drops the subquery — acceptance requires no ERROR, rows = 0, **and** a relaxed-predicate discriminating probe that is non-empty on PG, shipped as a unit test. | **EXECUTED 2026-07-29 — the pre-registered root cause above is REFUTED by direct measurement of the planned tree, and D1/D2/D3 were not the fix (see the doc's §0 and §R).** The failing ref is not an unrepaired `ColumnRef` in a `Filter` below the subquery's `Project`; it is the subquery's **own `Project` target**, which `remapSubqueryColumnRefs` had already numbered **correctly** (`ca_zip/0`) and which a LATER pass overwrote. That pass is `applyJoinTreePosMap` (`bushy.go`), which descended into any `Project` not flagged `IsolatedScope` and remapped its targets with the **outer** bindings' position map — a map defined only over the space `buildBindingsPosMap`'s `collect` walked, and `collect` stops at *every* join-tree `Project` ("Extend it to all Projects … and stop"). `posMap(0)` matched the outer binding starting at 0 (`store_sales`) and returned its **MHJ-reordered** offset — so 57 is a join-order offset, the signature of this pass, not the "global FROM-order index" the ledger read it as. The build half was generalised to all `Project`s and the apply half was not: CLAUDE.md's "sibling paths must change together", and the mirror image of `9740fce9`, which taught `collect` to step *past* a `SetOp` while leaving this applier free to walk into the scope above it. Fix = stop at every join-tree `Project`; nothing is lost, since the inner plan is already normalised by `remapSubqueryColumnRefs` and Projects *above* the join tree belong to `remapTopProjection`, and it cannot disable the outer remap because a `Project` root already yielded a `nil` posMap. V0's acceptance bar was honoured in full: a **non-empty** doll-house probe (`alpha\|5`, `beta\|7`) verified byte-identical on **PostgreSQL 18.3**, shipped as two tests — a planner structural invariant (every `Project` target addresses its own child) and an executor value probe — **both proved to FAIL pre-fix** with `ca_zip/6 … out of MaterializedSlot range 1`, plus a shape guard that skips loudly if the defective plan stops being produced. **Residual deferred:** removing the error unmasks the plan's true cost — the `substr` residual sits on a cross join above the full three-way MHJ with `d_qoy`/`d_year` unpushed — so Q8 leaves the ERROR class and joins the **timeout class** (measured: exceeded a 1500 s budget at SF0.5, elapsed 1633 s, where it previously errored at ~11 s). Not a regression from this change, which alters one `ColumnRef` index and no plan shape. |

time it explicitly and raise the budget for the acceptance run rather than reporting a regression. **Gate visibility is measured, not assumed, and is not uniform**: at HEAD the SF0.5 gate sees only Q47 (`MISMATCH 43s`) — Q49 and Q51 both flipped to `PASS` there the moment M0125-0009 landed, which nothing recorded, and neither has been re-measured at SF=1 since; that is why -0014/-0015 are written as "re-measure, then resolve or classify". `ci/batch/tpcds-row-anchors.csv` pins 61 queries and contains **none** of the three, so closing any of them means adding an anchor rather than re-pinning one, and Q47/Q51 carry `ck=n/a` in the SF0.5 oracle so value acceptance is SF=1 only. **✅ UPDATE 2026-07-30 — two of the three defects are gone, closed by measurement at STEP 0.** Re-measured at SF=1 on HEAD `f3f31d87` (`analysis/m0125-0014-0015-q49-q51-sf1/`): **Q49 = `OK 83 s / 34 rows`** (`ck=63ace0d888e86982`, value-diff `RENDERING-ONLY (numeric scale)`) and **Q51 = `OK 47 s / 100 rows`** (`ck=443e242cfab22c02`, `RENDERING-ONLY (bpchar/width)`), both value-equal to PG — so the 3 × 10 `OR`-collapse arithmetic, the `decimal(15,4)` precision candidate and the outer-join-plus-comma-join shape all describe a row count goopg no longer produces, and **Q51's 13 s budget margin is retired** (553 s of headroom at 47 s; The runtime half therefore needs no Q47-specific task; Q47 is simply the sharpest benchmark witness for that deferral (159× PG, and what pushes it past the SF0.5 gate's 300 s cap on *half* the data). | 0125-0034 | [A join over a set operation stops being a Cartesian product (M0125-0034, C1 set-operation arm)](0125-0034-setop-join-promotion.md) | **set-operation arm implemented 2026-07-31; CTE/derived-aggregate arm open** | `M0125-0026`'s dominant timeout mechanism: `Nested Loop (CROSS)` with the equi-join demoted to a `Filter` wherever a join input was a subquery.
